subcategory: native shrub grown for winter stem color

planting.note: Set container or bare-root stock into consistently moist soil in early spring or fall; the golden bark deepens in color over each shrub's second and third winters.

directions: Grow in evenly moist to wet, humus-rich soil, siting in full sun for the most saturated chartreuse-to-gold stem color through winter, since shaded plants tend to hold a duller olive tone. Flat clusters of small white flowers open in late spring and are followed by whitish berries that draw songbirds, but the shrub is grown chiefly for its bare winter wood. Because color intensity fades on older bark, cut one-third of the thickest canes to the ground each early spring to keep a steady supply of young golden stems. The colony spreads by suckering and works well massed along streambanks or as a season-spanning backdrop where winter interest is wanted at a distance.

common_name: Sibirica Siberian Dogwood (Coral-Red Winter Stem Dogwood)
subcategory: deciduous shrub grown for winter stem color

planting.note: Plant container stock in moist, humus-rich soil in spring or fall; stems show their strongest coral-red hue starting the second winter after planting.

directions: Plant in reliably moist, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, giving this selection open exposure through winter so the coral-red bark can color to its deepest intensity against snow. Small white flower clusters in late spring give way to bluish-white summer berries, but the shrub earns its place for the vivid bare stems once autumn leaves drop. Renewal-prune one-third of the oldest, palest canes to the ground every spring, since the brightest bark forms only on wood one to three years old. Its slightly more restrained size and habit than the wild species make it a tidier choice for foundation plantings and pond-edge borders.

common_name: Elegantissima Variegated Tatarian Dogwood (Silver-Margined Red-Stem Dogwood)
subcategory: deciduous shrub grown for variegated foliage and winter stem color

planting.note: Set out container stock in consistently moist soil in spring or fall; full variegation develops fully by the second growing season.

directions: Grow in moist, humus-rich soil with partial shade to protect the gray-green, white-margined leaves from summer scorch, which is more of a concern here than on green-leaved dogwoods. The creamy leaf edges brighten a shaded border all season, then drop in autumn to reveal the deep red winter stems that give the plant its second season of interest. Cut one-third of the oldest stems to the ground each early spring, which both refreshes bark color and encourages the largest, most cleanly variegated new foliage. Watch for any shoots reverting to solid green and remove them at the base promptly, since reverted growth is more vigorous and will overtake the variegated wood if left.

common_name: Kelseyi Dwarf Red-Twig Dogwood (Compact Winter-Stem Dogwood)
subcategory: native dwarf shrub grown for winter stem color

planting.note: Set container plants into moist, well-drained soil in spring or fall; this compact selection fills in as a low colony within two to three seasons.

directions: Plant in moist, average to rich soil in full sun for the deepest red winter bark, though this dwarf selection tolerates considerably more shade than taller red-twig types. Its naturally low, dense, mounded habit needs no shearing to stay compact, making it useful as a foreground planting or low informal hedge in front of taller winter-interest shrubs. Because the plant stays small, renewal pruning can be lighter than on full-size red-osier dogwood: remove only the oldest, dullest stems at the base every second or third spring to keep color fresh. It spreads gradually by short stolons, tolerating occasional wet soil and forming a tidy colony well suited to rain gardens and pond margins.
